title: Serializing a tree
sub: Pre-order with null markers and one cursor on the way back; a string versus bytes; an object graph in Unity
cards/0/body:
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (LeetCode #297, hard). Write two methods: serialize(root) turns a binary tree into a string, deserialize(data) turns that string back into the very same tree. The format is up to you. Up to 10⁴ nodes, values from −1000 to 1000, and they may repeat.

Signals: “encode / decode”, “save and load”, “send over the network”. A structure with references has to be laid out as a flat sequence so that its shape comes back unambiguously. So the sequence must carry not only the values but also the shape: where a branch ends.

The format LeetCode uses to write trees — [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] — is already a serialization: a level-order walk where null marks a missing child and trailing nulls are dropped. Here node 2 has no children (two nulls), and node 3 has children 4 and 5.
cards/1/title: Why one traversal is not enough
cards/1/body:
The first impulse is to write the values out with some traversal. But a traversal without markers loses the shape. The trees “2 with 1 on the left” and “1 with 2 on the right” give the same in-order: 1, 2. Pre-order without markers is ambiguous too: “2 with 1 on the left” and “2 with 1 on the right” both give 2, 1.

Two traversals together — pre-order and in-order — do rebuild a tree (#105), but only when the values are distinct: the subtree root is located in the in-order by its value. Here values repeat, and in a tree of all ones there is no telling which one is the root. And writing the tree twice doubles the size.

The conclusion: the shape must be written explicitly — mark every place where a child is missing.
cards/1/code:
// different trees — the same in-order: 1, 2
var a = new TreeNode(2, left: new TreeNode(1));    //   2       1
var b = new TreeNode(1, right: new TreeNode(2));   //  /         \
                                                   // 1           2
cards/2/q: A BST with distinct keys is serialized as a single in-order, with no markers. Is that enough to rebuild the tree?
cards/2/options/0: No: the in-order of every BST with these keys is the same sorted list
cards/2/options/1: Yes: in a BST the in-order determines the tree uniquely
cards/2/options/2: Yes, since the keys are distinct
cards/2/options/3: No, but only if some keys are negative
cards/2/explain: In-order visits a BST in ascending order (trees unit), so every BST built from these keys has the same in-order — the sorted list — and the shape is lost entirely. Pre-order of a BST without markers, however, is unambiguous (#449): the first key is the root, the smaller keys after it form the left subtree, the larger ones the right subtree.
cards/2/wrong/1: The keys 1, 2, 3 give several different BSTs: a chain to the right, a chain to the left, root 2 with two children… All of them have in-order 1, 2, 3.
cards/2/wrong/2: Distinct keys help the pair pre-order + in-order. A single in-order of a BST is always just the sorted keys.
cards/2/wrong/3: The sign of the numbers has nothing to do with it: it is the shape that gets lost, not the values.
cards/3/title: Pre-order with markers and a single cursor
cards/3/body:
Write the tree in pre-order — the node's value, then its left subtree, then its right subtree — and put a marker # in place of every missing child. The tree [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] becomes 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#.

Why it is unambiguous. Every value is followed by exactly two subtrees, and a subtree is either # or a value with its own two subtrees. Reading left to right, you always know what starts next. n nodes have 2n child slots, n − 1 of them filled, so there are n + 1 markers and 2n + 1 tokens in total.

Reading mirrors writing: Read takes the token under the cursor; # — return null; a number — create a node and recursively read its left subtree, then its right. There is one cursor for the whole recursion, and it only moves forward — in C# that is ref int pos or a class field. Time is O(n) both ways, memory is O(n) for the string and O(h) for the recursion stack.
cards/4/q: The string 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,#. Which tree is it in LeetCode format?
cards/4/options/3: The string is invalid: there are too few markers
cards/4/explain: 1 is the root; then its left subtree: 2 and two # — a leaf. Then the right one: 3, with 4 on its left (two # again) and # on its right. By levels: 1; 2 and 3; 2 has no children, 3 has a left child 4. Check: 4 values and 5 markers — exactly n + 1.
cards/4/wrong/1: [1, 2, 3, 4] puts 4 as the left child of 2. But 2 is followed immediately by two # — it has no children.
cards/4/wrong/2: Then 1 would be followed by # (no left child). In the string 1 is followed by 2 — that is the left subtree.
cards/4/wrong/3: 4 values and 5 markers — exactly n + 1, the string is complete.
cards/5/explain: A marker goes where null is. The left subtree first, then the right: the same order as reading. The cursor is passed by reference, otherwise every call moves its own copy. pos++ takes the current token and advances the cursor; ++pos would skip the very first token — the root.
cards/6/task: Walk both phases on the tree [5, 3, 8, null, 4, 7]: first writing to a string, then reading it back with one cursor. The rig will ask once in each phase.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: 5,3 is written. Which token does the code write next?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: Pre-order: after node 3 comes its left subtree, and 3 has no left child: write #. Then the right subtree of 3 — that is 4 — and only once the whole subtree of 3 is written does the root's right child, 8, come.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: 5, 3, # have been read. The cursor is on token 4. Where does Read attach node 4?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: # closed the left subtree of 3: that call returned null, and Read for node 3 moved on to node.right = Read(…). The next token starts the right subtree of 3. The right subtree of 5 begins only after markers close the subtree of 3 — at the seventh token, 8.
cards/7/q: On the string 1,2,#,#,3,#,# this code returned a tree where both children of 1 are nodes 2, and node 3 is missing. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: pos is passed by value: every call moves its own copy, and the caller never learns about the advance. The left call for 1 read 2, #, #, but the root's cursor stayed at token 1 — so the right call reads 2 again. The cursor must be shared: ref int pos (and ref on every call) or a class field.
cards/8/body:
A string is readable and handy for debugging, but expensive: StringBuilder grows by doubling, ToString copies, Split creates an array and 2n + 1 token strings, int.Parse parses each one. At 10⁴ nodes that is tens of thousands of heap objects. Without Split you can parse in place: ReadOnlySpan<char> and int.Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>, …) exist in .NET Standard 2.1 too.

Bytes. A BinaryWriter over a MemoryStream, or a Span<byte> with BinaryPrimitives (System.Buffers.Binary, available in Unity as well): a number is 4 bytes, and nothing needs parsing. But the marker now has to be encoded: if values can be any int, there is no “spare” value for null. The fix is a flag byte before each node: 1 — a value follows, 0 — null. Or a bit mask of the shape stored apart from the values.

Set the byte order explicitly (WriteInt32LittleEndian), and put a version number at the start of the format: saves must survive a game update.
cards/8/deep:
Depth. A chain of 10⁴ nodes means 10⁴ nested calls in both Write and Read. On the main thread with a 1 MB stack that usually passes, but at 10⁵–10⁶ nodes or on a thread with a small stack you get a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught. Writing without recursion uses an explicit Stack<TreeNode>: pop a node, write it, push the right child, then the left. Reading without recursion uses a stack of “node and which child comes next”.

By levels. LeetCode's format is a valid answer too: a breadth-first walk with a queue, null in place of a missing child. Reading uses a queue of parents: each next token is the left, then the right child of the next parent. Also 2n + 1 tokens before trimming the tail and O(n), and recursion depth is no concern.

More compact. Small numbers are written with variable length: 7 bits per byte, the high bit meaning “another byte follows” (varint). In .NET 5+ this is the public BinaryWriter.Write7BitEncodedInt; in Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) it is protected, so you write your own loop. The shape can be stored as bits: 2n + 1 bits instead of flag bytes.
cards/9/q: Node values can be any int. Someone proposes writing null as int.MinValue in the binary format. What is wrong?
cards/9/options/0: A node with the value int.MinValue becomes null after loading: the full int range has no spare value
cards/9/options/1: Nothing: int.MinValue never occurs in trees
cards/9/options/2: int.MinValue does not fit into 4 bytes
cards/9/options/3: It works, but only with big-endian byte order
cards/9/explain: A marker must differ from every possible value. When values cover the whole int range, that is impossible within the same 4 bytes — you need a separate flag. In #297 values are from −1000 to 1000, and a “magic” number would work there, but that leans on the constraints, and you should say so out loud.
cards/9/wrong/1: “Never occurs” until it does: damage, a coordinate, an id. A format that breaks on a valid value is a bug.
cards/9/wrong/2: An int is exactly 4 bytes, int.MinValue = 0x80000000 included.
cards/9/wrong/3: Byte order changes the layout, not the set of values: no spare value appears.
cards/10/title: Unity: an object graph with references
cards/10/body:
A game save is not a tree but a graph: a quest references an NPC, two units reference the same squad, the squad references its units back. Unity's serializer stores a field of a [Serializable] class by value by default, right inside its owner. Hence: null is not preserved (it becomes an object with empty fields); two references to one object become two copies after loading; a field of the class's own type — left and right on a tree node — is silently skipped by Unity; indirect cycles are cut off at depth 10 with a warning.

[SerializeReference] stores such fields by reference: every object gets an id within its host object (a MonoBehaviour, a ScriptableObject), and the field records that id. null, polymorphism, shared references and cycles all work — but only within one host: a reference cannot be shared between two assets.

Your own save format does the same by hand: ids instead of references. Every object gets a number, and a reference is written as that number. While writing, an “object → id” dictionary marks visited objects, otherwise a cycle would loop the writer forever. Loading takes two passes: first create every object, then wire up the references by number. The second pass is what handles cycles: by the time you link, all objects already exist.
cards/11/q: What is true about saving an object graph in Unity? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: Without [SerializeReference], two references to one [Serializable] object become two copies after loading
cards/11/options/1: [SerializeReference] preserves null, polymorphism and cycles within one host object
cards/11/options/2: With your own format, loading takes two passes: create the objects, then link them by id
cards/11/options/3: [SerializeReference] shares one object between two different ScriptableObjects
cards/11/options/4: Pre-order with # markers saves any graph, cycles included
cards/11/explain: By value, every reference is written as its own copy. [SerializeReference] gives an object an id, but only within its host — there are no shared references across assets. # markers describe a tree: in a graph with shared nodes the walk writes a node twice, and on a cycle it never stops. A graph needs ids and visited marks.
cards/12/q: You are solving Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: do values repeat, what is their range, is the format free
cards/12/items/1: Explain why one traversal without markers is not enough: the shape is lost
cards/12/items/2: The idea: pre-order with # in place of null — every value is followed by exactly two subtrees
cards/12/items/3: Write serialize and deserialize with one cursor over the tokens
cards/12/items/4: Walk an example: write a small tree and read the string back
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n) both ways, 2n + 1 tokens, O(h) stack
cards/12/items/6: Improvements: a binary format with flags, a format version, a traversal without recursion
cards/12/explain: Repeated values are the first question: they rule out the “pre-order + in-order” idea right away. Then why markers are needed, the idea, the code, a round trip. Improvements at the end show that you are thinking about a real save format, not just the puzzle.
